title: Dr. Daddy-O (Vernon Winslow) and his rise on WBOK
summary: Tex recounts how Vernon Winslow, coaching white DJ Duke Thiel, got on the air, was sponsored by Jax beer, rose to fame, moved to WMRY and later declined.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: All righty. You know, Ted, I think it's about time that we start talking about a young man who had one of the greatest radio trademarks ever in history.
Let me kind of billboard this. January 1, no, January the 10th, 1996. This is real number two with Tex Stephens. Okay. Now we can do that.

Ted, we were getting ready to talk about when Winslow was better known as Dr. Daddio on the radio for too many people. Dr. Daddio, as he was widely known, was a very prolific art teacher at Dillon University. He had a beautiful command of the English language. And as they said, that Dr. Daddio would let it all hang out. So what really happened, he and Tom, in fact, Tom Newman was a marketing technician with one of the advertising agencies here in the city of New Orleans. This is how Dr. Daddio really got on the radio. But prior to that, Vernon was very aggressive. He wasn't born in New Orleans. He was born someplace up in Ohio. But Vernon was working part-time, feeding information to a fellow by the name of Duke Thiel, who was a white disc jockey, who was working on W, I'm trying to think of the call letters of that station. No, it wasn't an N-O-E or was it N-N-R? It wasn't an R. It wasn't even going there. It was WW, well, whatever. We'll eventually get the call letters. We've had so many here in the city of New Orleans. So anyway, Vernon was, I do feel being white, did not know the lingo as to how blacks would exchange ideas like what's happening, baby, down it and down it and get around it. Everything is tough. Hang tough, baby. What's happening? What's going down? What's in the alley, man? What you know? Everything is on the hook. Well, beating it down to a little goose upon us on another QT. What's the sound from around town? Well, see, Duke Thiel didn't understand that was black lingo. Where you're at? What's happening? You know, things like that. Everything is cool, baby. The last order from across the border, that was Dr. Daddy was spooked. All this kind of stuff, you see. And what really happened, Daddy was really schooling him as to how, when he played his records, because Duke Thiel was the most popular white disc jockey directed toward the black market at that time on this station. And Dr. Daddy was in the background teaching him or instructing him as to how to relate and interrelate when he plays black music and how to talk about it. You know? All right. Well, so it just so happened that nobody heard Vernon on the radio. Vernon would, in fact, it was at the Old Jam Hotel where they were broadcasting from. And when Vernon went there, he didn't went through the front door. He went up on the freight elevator, which is a damn shame at that time. So, eventually, somewhere in time, one day Duke Thiel showed up late, and the program was supposed to go on the air. And nothing happened. Somehow or another, accidentally, the mics came open some kind of way, and there was Vernon for about maybe two minutes, a minute and a half to waiting for Duke to come. So, thanks to Duke showed up. Well, Vernon lost his job the next fifteen, twenty minutes, and they fired him. Well, Tom Newman, who, like I said, was working for an advertising agency at that time and heard about this incident, he made contact with Vernon back at Dill University. And eventually, they started coming up with commercial advertising for a program. So, what he did, he went to the Jackson Brewing Company, which is probably the most popular beer in New Orleans at that time, because it was manufactured here. Because at that time, you had 4X, you had Union Beer, you had Rico Beer, you had Falstaff Beer, they all were manufactured here. Boy, New Orleans was in its really glory at that time. And, uh, so somehow or another, Jack's Beer decided to sponsor Dr. Dario on the radio. And boy, all of a sudden, New Orleans exploded with recorded music because he would start, like, around about 6 or 6.30 after the news would come off the radio, and then he would play his music and so forth. So, Vernon got so dark on Popula until Jack said, well, look, let's move him around from ballroom to ballroom where they sell our products. Let him sign autographs. And that's how I really first met Vernon in the ballroom, signing autographs. And so, uh, eventually, he became very, very popular. And, uh, they, uh, started, uh, going from ball to ball, lounge to lounge with Vernon, uh, you know, signing the autographs and talking about his music. And, uh, that's how it all started. And, uh, eventually, uh, what happened, uh, he was on, oh, I think Vernon started on WBOK in 1950, 50, and 1951. I think it was 1950, 51 that he really started. And, uh, eventually, uh, I'm trying to think, uh, the management of WBOK at that time started buying, uh, other radio stations across the country. And they bought a station, uh, over in Houston, Texas. And, uh, they sent a fella from, uh, New Orleans by the name of Spurdy Johnson to open a station up there. And Spurdy became the first black disc jockey in Houston, Texas. It was so popular until they really started stretching out all over there. And I think he started calling himself Hotsy Totsy over in Houston, Texas, which was an offshoot of Dr. Daddy O'Brien Winslow here in the city of New Orleans. But New Orleans, like I said, has given, uh, birth to so many fads, so many disc jockeys, so many cultured things from Lewis Armstrong on down to many people who have gotten lost in history until we start talking about it. And we start, uh, getting into, uh, from religion to entertainment to stage plays to music. You name it. I could name a lot of people into many fields who made tremendous contributions to the city of New Orleans to the United States of America. But, uh, all in all, uh, when you get back to Vernon Winslow, uh, he, uh, Dr. Daddy Rayson was widely acclaimed. Uh, somewhere in time, uh, the Jackson Brewing Company was beginning to have financial problems. Uh, I don't know, at that time, let me tell you what was happening. Uh, here, here I got involved, a fellow by the name of, uh, Billy Willis had called me one day because I was a disc jockey on, on, uh, old, uh, old WMRY, which was the rival station of WVOK. Now, I was working part time, but Vernon Winslow was on every day. That's why he got more popular than me and Ernest Whip. Now, Ernest Whip was on every day was between Ernest Whip and, uh, Dr. Daddy Oak and so forth and so on to compete against, uh, one another. Uh, but, uh, here, here's what happened to Jackson Brewing Company at that time. We're sponsoring, uh, live football, baseball broadcasts from the various high schools in the city of New Orleans. And that's when, uh, uh, myself and, uh, Mel Levitt started broadcasting live television football games from right back there at Savvy. And also at City Park and so forth and so on. So Jack's had it all, had it all together at that time. Somewhere along, away from what I understand. The management hired a New York marketing and advertising firm to probably strategize or extend Jack's out of New Orleans, geographically, all across the country. And something didn't gel right. And with the competition, Fall Staff and Slits and other power beers at that time. Uh, Pabst Blue Ribbon. Well, they just didn't make it, I think. The agency was overcharging Jack's. They didn't understand high power brokering and, uh, the new structure from Wall Street. They started losing money and they started all fighting among themselves. That's the way it was told to me. And, uh, so Vernon, eventually staying in radio, gravitated over to, uh, WMRY and became very popular. Now, here's what happened. He changed from, uh, popular music, uh, going into the spiritual aspect of music. And that was another, uh, structure that Vernon got into. He was still called Dr. Daddy-O. Darius D Somewhere in time, the management and the station were sold, and they brought in new people from out of town who bought the station. And they set up a new infrastructure inside the station. And they had a young lady there, she started needling Vernon, and eventually she got into his mind or some kind of way, and he decided to leave the station. And believe you me, I think that kind of really messed with his mind, because something happened to him. It was kind of psyched out after all his great contributions as a teacher and as an information specialist on radio and generating a new point of information in the city of New Orleans, from a cultured and intellectual point of view, and an informative point of view. That kind of got to Vernon and he started, like he started losing his mind or something started happening to him, because they were contemplating on having a date for him, because Jim Hutchison had called me, but somehow or another, it just fell by the wayside. He never got around to it. The next time I know Vernon was in the hospital, it's a good reason I heard he had died, and we funeralized him just a couple of years ago, and that was it. But, yeah, I just can't cover everything about Vernon. Really, he never was a guy who really hung in bars as such. He only went in bars because he was so directed by the people who paid his salary, Jackson Brewing Company, no matter of advertisers he had on the air, because he was not a drinking or a smoking man. Vernon was a very handsome young man, very attractive, and he had beautiful mannerisms. He was not there, but he was really, he's more of a socialite. In fact, sometimes, as I look back at Vernon and listen to him, sometimes I think he was out of place, or played, like that kind of music. Yeah, when you meet Vernon and you listen to what he did on radio, you kind of feel like,
is this the guy I was listening to on radio?
Yeah, he's really a cultured individual.
